Also, genetics aren't that simple. Think like colourblindness: If a trait is recessive and X-linked, weird things can happen. If you're male and marry a colourblind woman, all of your male offspring will be colourblind (because they inherited her X, and both have the recessive colourblind gene). And if you're colourblind and male, all of your female children will be (at minimum) carriers of the colourblind gene... But you can't guarantee they will be colourblind, because they still receive an X from their mother, so unless she's a carrier or colourblind, your female children will only be carriers.

There's also things called (IIRC) "[de-]activator genes". If you look at ligers, they tend to be larger than either parent. This is because of a genetic war that happens between parents: Male genes do everything they can to make the offspring big, so that it will be strong and successful. Meanwhile, female genes do their best to make the offspring small, so that it can be birthed easier. In addition to creating genes that mean "big" or "small", they also make genes that target the "big/small" genes offered by the other parent. Well... Those "big/small" genes are different in tigers than in lions, so when you make a hybrid, the deactivator genes don't have a target, so all of the big genes get activated instead of only some, and you're left with a giant liger cub as a result.
